segments.text: Welcome to unintended consequences, episode 56 for July 12, 2026.
Today's story is one of those rare examples where the cure was almost worse than the disease,
at least at first. In a Manila office tower in 2017, a contractor named Liza sat before a
screen that refreshed every few seconds with videos of beheadings, sexual assaults, and live
suicides. She had been hired to keep Facebook's newsfeed free of graphic content for users
in the United States and Europe. The company's engineers had built automated filters that caught
obvious spam and nudity, yet every day thousands of edge cases still required human judgment.
The system worked exactly as designed. The platform stayed fast, and the visible workforce stayed small.
The harm simply moved down the supply chain. In the mid-2000s, executives at Facebook, YouTube,
and Twitter faced an obvious problem. User-generated content was growing faster than any central team
could review. They wanted the platforms to feel welcoming enough that ordinary people would post
photos of their children and share news without encountering gore or abuse. Automated tools could
handle volume, but they could not yet interpret context, sarcasm or new forms of harm.
Outsourcing routine review to specialized contractors in lower cost countries therefore looked
like a rational, even responsible way to scale safety while keeping product teams focused on growth.
At the time, labor markets in the Philippines, India, and Kenya already supplied English
speaking graduates for call center and data entry work. Extending that model to content moderation
seemed like a straightforward extension of existing practice. By 2012, Facebook had begun routing
a large share of its most disturbing reports to Accenture and other business process firms in Manila
and Hyderabad. YouTube followed a similar pattern after its 2006 acquisition by Google and Twitter
relied on contractors in Ireland and the Philippines. Early metrics looked encouraging.
Average review time per item dropped. Removal rates for reported child exploitation material rose
above 95% in some categories. Public dashboards showed steady improvement. Company spokespeople
described the contractors as specialized safety teams and emphasized that the work protected
millions of users. A few internal memos and contractor handbooks warned that reviewers would see graphic
violence and recommended short breaks. Yet the dominant message remained that the work was manageable
with standard wellness programs. The labor model relied on peace rate pay and strict throughput
targets, often 100 to 150 items per hour. Because the most graphic material could not be fully
automated, the same workers saw repeated images of torture, rape, and death for 8 to 10 hours a day.
Within two or three years, clinicians in the Philippines began documenting clusters of anxiety,
depression, and post-traumatic stress symptoms among the contractor workforce.
A 2018 investigation by Casey Newton at the Verge described moderators who kept trauma folders
of the worst videos they could not unsee. Some reported nightmares that continued after they left the
job. The causal chain was direct. The promise of a clean product for end users required
continuous human exposure to the very material the product was meant to exclude. High turnover meant
constant retraining, which lowered average experience levels and increased errors. In 2020,
a group of canyon moderators sued meta and its outsourcing partner, alleging inadequate mental
health support. The case settled in 2021 with undisclosed terms and a commitment to provide counseling.
Similar claims surfaced in the United States against Cognizant, which had run Facebook
moderation centers in Arizona and Texas. Estimates from industry analysts placed the global
contractor workforce at roughly 100,000 people by 2019. Yet almost none of those costs appeared on
the platform's public balance sheets. After the reporting and litigation, several firms added onsite
counselors reduced shift links for the most graphic cues and began testing more granular
classification tools. Meta announced in 2022 that it would bring a larger share of moderation
in-house in some regions and would publish annual transparency reports on contractor welfare.
Automated systems have improved, especially for known child sexual abuse material.
But every major platform still routes difficult cases to humans. The new layer of oversight
itself created fresh frictions. Strictor mental health protocols sometimes slowed review cues,
prompting complaints from advocacy groups that harmful content stayed visible longer.
Today, the work continues in hybrid form, with contractors in lower cost locations still handling
the majority of first-pass decisions, while the platform's experiment with better filters and
occasional on-shore teams. When a product's quality depends on invisible human labor,
the true cost of that labor tends to be discovered only after harm accumulates.
Incentive structures that reward speed and low visible headcount will locate the difficult work
wherever wages and regulatory scrutiny are lowest. Complex systems, therefore,
require deliberate accounting for second-order human effects rather than assuming automation
or outsourcing will remain invisible. The same pattern appears today in the training of large
language models, where low-paid annotators label toxic texts so that end users encounter fewer harms.
The question for any organization scaling a digital service is therefore straightforward.
Once the difficult work is made visible, who bears its cost and how is that cost measured before
